# Field fortification (marching camp, wagon fort, entrenchment) (`field_fortification`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by surveying_triangulation, handguns_muskets
- Core idea: A ditch, the bank made from its spoil and a palisade or line of chained wagons turn open ground into a fortress within hours. It stops surprise, stops cavalry, gives missile troops time to shoot and gives a beaten army somewhere to rally. The Roman army dug a standard camp every night on the march, always to the same plan so that every man knew his place in the dark. Firearms made the method decisive: slow-loading gunners behind a ditch or wagons defeat charging cavalry and pikes.
- Pitfalls:
  - Treating digging as cowardice or as work for slaves; Roman legionaries dug their own camp daily
  - An entrenched army can be starved or bypassed if it has no water, food and line of retreat
  - A wagon fort is helpless against field artillery, which ended the Hussite method
  - A ditch that cannot be swept by the defenders' own missiles is cover for the attacker
- History: rome: by 2nd c. BC – daily marching camp described by Polybius; 52 BC – Caesar's double ring of 15 and 21 km at Alesia; china: 2nd–1st c. BC – Han frontier walls, watchtowers and fire signals; 16th c. – Qi Jiguang's war wagons against the Mongols; europe: 1420s – Hussite wagon forts (Jan Žižka) with handguns and light cannon; 1503 – Cerignola, arquebusiers behind a ditch defeat French cavalry and Swiss pikes; islamic: 1440s – Ottomans adopt the wagon fort (tabur cengi) from the Hungarians; used at Chaldiran 1514 and Mohács 1526; india: 1526 – Babur's carts and guns at Panipat on the Ottoman model; americas: 1864–1865 – trench lines at Petersburg foreshadow 1914–1918
- Read:
  - Polybius, Histories VI.27–42
  - Gábor Ágoston, Guns for the Sultan (2005)
  - Bert S. Hall, Weapons and Warfare in Renaissance Europe (1997)
